name: Chiropractic BioPhysics (CBP) cervical lordosis
lead: Chiropractic BioPhysics (CBP) is a posture-focused chiropractic technique founded in 1980 by Donald Harrison, Deanne Harrison and Daniel Murphy. It uses mathematical models of ideal spinal curves and combines adjustments, exercises and traction to restore them [1]. Cervical lordosis, the natural forward curve of the neck, is one of its main targets.

For appearance, the interest is in neck and head posture: a restored curve is meant to bring the head back over the shoulders and reduce the forward-head, rounded-shoulder look, which gives a straighter profile, a longer-looking neck and a more upright stance. Forward head posture is described as the ear sitting ahead of the shoulder line with the chin pushed forward [2].

Proponents also claim that restoring the curve reduces pain and improves function. A 2005 review of CBP publications, written within the chiropractic field, rated CBP evidence as comparable to spinal manipulation for neck pain [3], and a 2017 randomized trial reported that adding Denneroll extension traction to a multimodal program increased cervical lordosis in patients [4]. Grokipedia notes that critics question whether curve deviations relate to symptoms and point to the affiliation of many study authors with CBP [1].

paras: CBP uses a Harrison Spinal Model that describes the cervical curve as a circular arc and defines target angles [1]. Its signature approach, called Mirror Image, positions the patient opposite to their abnormal posture [1]. Sustained extension traction, typically 10 to 20 minutes per session, and foam orthotics such as the Denneroll are used in clinic and at home [1]. Cervical traction protocols were refined by Deed Harrison between 1996 and 2000 [1].

Forward head posture places the head forward of the shoulders and is often paired with rounded shoulders, a combination sometimes called upper crossed syndrome; it is associated in the literature with phone and computer use [2]. A review of the literature found cervical lordosis values to be significantly associated with thoracic kyphosis values, and rounded shoulders with increased thoracic kyphosis [5]. CBP treats the neck curve as part of a whole-spine model, so its programs also address head translation and upper-back posture [1].

A 2005 review of Clinical Biomechanics of Posture publications, the earlier name for CBP, compared controlled trials of CBP and spinal manipulation; it rated CBP evidence as roughly equal to spinal manipulation for neck pain and above the diversified technique taught in chiropractic colleges, and proposed a structural rehabilitation protocol [3].

A 2017 randomized controlled trial in 72 patients aged 40 to 55 with cervicogenic dizziness, a hypolordotic neck and anterior head translation compared a multimodal program with the same program plus Denneroll cervical traction; the traction group showed greater improvement in cervical lordosis, pain, head repositioning accuracy and dizziness outcomes at ten weeks and at one-year follow-up [4].

According to Grokipedia, a lateral X-ray study reported mean cervical angles of about 34.5 degrees in asymptomatic people, 28.6 in acute neck pain and 22.0 in chronic neck pain, and a non-randomized trial reported a 13.6 degree gain in C2-C7 Cobb angle with about 70 percent retention at 14 months [1]. Critics noted in the same source observe that curve deviations occur in many people without symptoms and that many trials are non-randomized and CBP-affiliated [1].

A rapid review cited by Grokipedia found no good evidence that routine spinal X-rays improve outcomes, raising radiation exposure questions, since CBP uses radiographs to measure curves [1]. Chiropractic neck manipulation in general has been linked to rare vertebral artery stroke, with disputed causality [6].

card.summary: Chiropractic traction and exercise system aiming to restore the neck curve; evidence is mostly from CBP-affiliated studies.
card.note: Relies on spinal X-rays; evidence mostly from affiliated authors.

quick.overview:
CBP is a chiropractic system that tries to restore the neck's forward curve (cervical lordosis) using traction, exercises and adjustments.

Most supporting studies come from CBP-affiliated authors, and critics question whether curve changes relate to symptoms.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners measure curves on X-rays and apply sustained extension traction, orthotics and Mirror Image positioning intended to produce lasting tissue change.
quick.risks: Repeated X-rays add radiation exposure, and neck manipulation has been associated with rare stroke. Certification is voluntary.

chain: Head carried further back over the shoulders
angle.text: CBP practitioners aim to reshape the neck curve so the head sits over the shoulders instead of forward of them. People seeking a more upright posture, a more defined neck line and a less forward-jutting chin use it for that outcome.
